\begin{abstract}
In April 2016 a House of Commons committee heard that new television rules from the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) would cost \lttvJobsTotal{} media jobs by 2020. The figure came from a commissioned economic-impact study detailed enough to check. I fixed the forecast record before collecting outcomes and compared the study's two scenarios with CRTC data for 2016--2019. The largest error was an input: the study assumed that \lttvByopSixteen{} of subscribers would take the entry-level package in 2016, rising to \lttvByopEighteen{}; the CRTC counted \lttvUptakeJuneShare{} by mid-2016. Specialty and pay channels' revenue, on which most of the job figure depends, stayed above the study's no-reform baseline, inconsistent with the forecast as made but consistent with the study's model run at actual uptake. Distributors' revenue was consistent with the forecast but fell more than that run predicts. Per-subscriber payments to Canadian channels outgrew even the study's no-reform path, and staffing didn't track its revenue chain in either sector. The testimony presented figures that depended on that assumption as unconditional job losses, called an economy-wide estimate, more than half of it spin-off, media jobs, and cited a share of programming spending that the study's own figures don't reproduce.
\end{abstract}

\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} forecast evaluation; ex post analysis; economic impact studies; broadcasting regulation; Canada
